items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: I think Dizzy, James Moody, Sonny Stitt, Wes Montgomery. I mean these are people that just were characters... It was fun watching Joe Williams because when he was doing “A Child is Born”...

ctx.x: Let’s talk about this conference we’re at. It’s an interesting state of affairs in jazz it seems like. If you come here — I just came from this little gathering of people talking about research. And in that room there was at least four or five different accents of people. In other words it was like an international group of people. And you’ve got I don’t know how many people here, and it makes jazz look really vibrant and healthy. And then you turn around and you read the typical “jazz is dead” article or — Gary…

Well he just doesn’t know. I don’t know why or even how or why he would even make such a statement because he obviously hasn’t been or doesn’t see the things that I see, and see what a lot of other — it’s a different time than when the music that even like what you presented with Joe Williams — that’s a different era. It was a different place. And even before that, that music was really popular. I mean the pop music of that day. We’ve lost that. I mean even Broadway, because a lot of those songs came through…

they weren’t all that — I mean nobody got rich off those clubs. They got a lot of notoriety that they could play, and you learned how to play. One of the things we’re missing is a network of going from state to state, city to city, to keep the music vibrant. The airlines, the economic — whatever you want to — has made it difficult. It still costs, if Miles Davis’ group was taking a flight to Paris, it costs the same for my group to go to Paris. And he’s making ten or twenty thousand times more money than I’m…
